content: Retinopathy is a term used to describe non-inflammatory damage to the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. This condition is most commonly caused by issues with the blood supply to the retina. Retinopathy often serves as an ocular manifestation of systemic diseases. The primary causes of retinopathy include the following: Diabetes, leading to diabetic retinopathy. Arterial hypertension, resulting in hypertensive retinopathy. Prematurity in newborns, which can cause retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). Sickle cell anemia, which can lead to retinal damage. Direct exposure to sunlight, causing solar retinopathy. Certain medications, leading to drug-induced retinopathy. Examples of such medications include hydroxychloroquine, interferon alfa-2b, tamoxifen, and trifluoperazine. Retinal vein or artery occlusion, which can impair blood flow to the retina. Many forms of retinopathy are progressive in nature. If left untreated, they can lead to severe vision loss, visual impairment, or even blindness, particularly when the macula, the central part of the retina responsible for detailed vision, is affected. Diagnosis of retinopathy is performed by an optometrist or ophthalmologist through a procedure called ophthalmoscopy, which involves examining the retina. The treatment approach depends on the underlying cause of the condition.
